stem: A 6-month-old full-term boy is brought to the emergency department with lethargy and vomiting.  The patient was breastfed exclusively until 2 days ago when homemade pureed food was added to his diet.  He has had no fever or diarrhea.  Examination shows a pale, diaphoretic, and ill-appearing infant.  Serum glucose is 30 mg/dL.  Diagnostic testing confirms aldolase B deficiency.  Which of the following should be removed from this patient's diet?​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌
explanation:
Hereditary fructose intolerance is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by aldolase B deficiency.  Aldolase B normally cleaves fructose-1-phosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde, which can be further metabolized through glycolysis.

With aldolase B deficiency, fructose ingestion leads to fructose-1-phosphate accumulation, which traps intracellular phosphate and depletes ATP.  This impairs glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, reducing hepatic glucose output and causing severe hypoglycemia (eg, lethargy, pallor, diaphoresis).  Vomiting is also common, and continued exposure can cause liver and kidney injury.

Sucrose is a disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose; its digestion releases fructose and therefore triggers symptoms.  Treatment requires avoidance of fructose, sucrose, and sorbitol (converted to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase).  Exclusively breastfed infants generally remain asymptomatic until fructose-containing foods are introduced (eg, fruit puree).

(Choices A and D)  Starch is the major storage carbohydrate in plants and consists of amylose (unbranched) and amylopectin (branched).  Both contain only glucose units.  Glucose and glucose-based carbohydrates do not produce fructose during digestion.

(Choice B)  Cellulose is a linear polysaccharide of glucose found in plant cell walls.  Humans lack the enzymes needed to digest its β-1,4 glycosidic bonds; it acts as insoluble dietary fiber and contributes to stool bulk.

(Choices C, E, and F)  Lactose, the principal carbohydrate in breast milk, consists of glucose and galactose.  Maltose consists of 2 glucose molecules.  Neither disaccharide releases fructose during digestion, and galactose metabolism does not require aldolase B.  Therefore, these sugars do not need to be excluded.  In contrast, infants with classic galactosemia typically develop jaundice, vomiting, and hepatomegaly shortly after breast milk or standard milk-based formula feeding begins.

Educational objective:Hereditary fructose intolerance results from aldolase B deficiency.  Fructose-1-phosphate accumulation traps phosphate and depletes ATP, impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and causing hypoglycemia after fructose ingestion.  Treatment requires avoidance of fructose, sucrose (glucose plus fructose), and sorbitol.​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌
